newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Mowlam brings optimism to tough job.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Mowlam brings optimism to tough job.

text.p: Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam is not short of the one thing needed for one of the most thankless jobs in British politics -- optimism.
She is the first woman to hold the job of bringing peace to Northern Ireland, a goal that has eluded her 10 male predecessors.

Now, after Saturday's announcement of an Irish Republican Amry ceasefire in its war against British rule, Mowlam faces the tough task of keeping the pro-British Unionists on side despite their intense suspicion of the nationalists' motives.
At the age of 47, she has enjoyed a rapid rise through the ranks of the Labour Party and was appointed to the Northern Ireland Office on Tony Blair's landslide May 1 election victory.

While nobody would suggest Mowlam will have an easy ride, Labour's massive parliamentary majority at least means she will not face the same difficulties as the Conservative government, which depended heavily on the goodwill of a handful of Unionist MPs to keep its grip on power.
Mowlam enjoyed a honeymoon with the province's nationalists in her early days in office, but she soon learned the harsh realities of Northern Ireland life.
A warm welcome from nationalists turned frosty after a leaked official document appeared to show that talks over a disputed Protestant march had been a sham.

She soon got into trouble with the pro-British Unionist side when the government was forced to disclose it had been in secret contacts with Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, despite a self-imposed ban on such overtures.
With a refreshingly personal touch, Mowlam was the antithesis of her remote and patrician predecessor, the Conservative Sir Patrick Mayhew.
She hit the headlines earlier in the year when it was disclosed she has been fighting a benign brain tumour.
This forced tabloid newspapers to backtrack on catty stories about her sudden weight gain and instead praise her quiet bravery.
At a meeting in Washington after a long hot day she astonished onlookers by removing the wig she wears to hide hair loss caused by her treatement.
A former academic, she entered parliament in 1987 and spoke for Labour on corporate affairs, culture and women's issues before making her name as opposition spokeswoman on Northern Ireland.
With a penchant for cigarettes and black coffee, and famous for her "spectacularly untidy" private life, Mowlam was eventually married in 1995 to Jon Norton, a divorced, socialist merchant banker.
She also made a name as someone prone to indiscretions, once suggesting that Buckingham Palace should be sold and Queen Elizabeth rehoused in a flat.
Those who have met her speak of her sex appeal and "an animated earthiness that leaves grown men spellbound".
She is the daughter of two Post Office workers. Her father was an alcoholic.
"Like my mother, I'm strong and pushy, a basically optimistic person," Mowlam once said.
The first test of her mettle since she was given the Northern Ireland portfolio came two weeks ago and the Roman Catholic nationalist community said she had failed it.
Police chiefs allowed the Protestant Orange Order to stage an annual parade on the Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
The result was some of the worst violence seen in years and so much criticism of Mowlam from the nationalists that she was forced to speak of her own "failure".

A further storm of nationalist protest burst over her with the publication of a leaked Northern Ireland Office document which appeared to show that a decision to allow the Orangemen along the Garvaghy Road had been taken well in advance.
The document, Mowlam's detractors claimed, showed that talks held before the march had been nothing but a sham.
Mowlam learned the hard way it is almost impossible to please both sides of the province's sectarian divide.
Mayhew often said: "If you upset both sides in Northern Ireland, you know you are getting it about right. If you upset one side, you are in trouble."
